US to make visa bond programme permanent for people from dozens of countries. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The US State Department will make permanent a visa bond programme that could require applicants from 50 countries, mostly from Africa, to post bonds of up to $20,000 when seeking US visas, according to a federal notice posted online on Friday.

The Federal Register notice applies to B1 and B2 visas, which are issued for business and tourism travel.

“Consular officers may require covered nonimmigrant visa applicants to post a bond of up to $20,000 as a condition of visa issuance, as determined by the consular officers,” the notice said.

“The 2025 visa bond pilot, which provided a framework for the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of the Treasury to assess the feasibility of administering a visa bond programme, has provided sufficient data to suggest that a visa bond programme is an effective tool for enforcing compliance among bonded visa holders.”

In the pilot programme, consular officers could require bonds of $5,000, $10,000 or up to $15,000. The final rule eliminates the $5,000 option and raises the maximum bond to $20,000.

The final rule goes into effect on August 3 when it is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register. In the list of 50 countries for whose citizens this programme applies, 30 are from Africa.

US officials say the policy is intended to reduce visa overstays. Immigration advocates argue it will deter legitimate travel to the United States.

Rights advocates say President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown violates free speech and due process, while creating an unsafe environment for ethnic minorities and encouraging racial profiling. Trump has defended the measures as necessary to bolster national security.

While Trump says he wants to curb illegal immigration, his administration has made legal immigration more difficult, for example, by imposing new and expensive fees for applicants of certain visas and by enforcing social media vetting for applicants and immigrants already in the country.

Earlier in May, the State Department identified nationals from the following 50 countries as being required to post visa bonds: Algeria, Angola, Antigua and Barbuda, Bangladesh, Benin, Bhutan, Botswana, Burundi, Cabo Verde, Cambodia, Central African Republic, Cote D’Ivoire, Cuba, Djibouti, Dominica, Ethiopia, Fiji, Gabon, The Gambia, Georgia, Grenada, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Kyrgyz Republic, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mongolia, Mozambique, Namibia, Nepal, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Papua New Guinea, Sao Tome and Principe, Senegal, Seychelles, Tajikistan, Tanzania, Togo, Tonga, Tunisia, Turkmenistan, Tuvalu, Uganda, Vanuatu, Venezuela, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

item.title: PPP, PML-N continue war of words on eve of Muzaffarabad elections. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The PPP and the PML-N continued lambasting each other on Saturday, extending their rhetoric from the ongoing elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) to the other party’s previous tenures in power.

The PPP and the PML-N — coalition partners in the Centre — have been engaged in a war of words since the PML-N emerged as the winner in the elections in AJK’s Mirpur division. The PPP has accused the PML-N of rigging in Mirpur and demanded re-polling.

The political temperatures remain heated as the second phase of AJK elections is set to be held tomorrow in nine constituencies of Muzaffarabad division. The third phase is scheduled for August 10 in all 12 refugee constituencies, and 11 constituencies of Poonch division.

In the latest exchange, PML-N senior leader Rana Sanaullah questioned the legitimacy of President Asif Ali Zardari’s role as he responded to PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s allegations of rigging in the 2024 general elections.

“If you call the votes secured by the prime minister votes of Forms-47, then on what forms has the president gotten votes on?” Sanaullah said.

On Wednesday, Bilawal had taken a direct jibe at Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, saying: “If someone is sitting on the PM’s seat, or someone is sitting on the CM’s position today, even a child knows that it is not because of the people’s votes or your performance but because of Form-47.”

Sanaullah, also the prime minister’s aide on political affairs and a federal minister, was addressing a gathering in Jhelum Valley alongside Kashmir Affairs Minister Amir Muqam.

Sanaullah further said: “If you say to Mian Nawaz Sharif that he became the prime minister for the first time or every time through rigging, […] then remember, it is also discussed here that someone also became the prime minister for the first time after breaking apart the country.”

He was referring to PPP founder Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who became the president of Pakistan in December 1971 after the secession of Bangladesh (then-East Pakistan) following the 1970 elections.

In August 1973, Bhutto took the oath as the prime minister in 1973 under the new Constitution.

Sanaullah also took a jibe at Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, whose recent remarks have sparked a fresh debate in political circles on the matter of creating new provinces.

Calling Naqvi a “blessed one” of President Zardari, the PML-N leader said the interior minister had “made the [political] journey of 30 years in three-and-a-half years”.

“You began from where and have now reached where, and now you realise that this system is completely dysfunctional.”

In his speech, Muqam criticised the PPP’s governance in Sindh, saying that no performance of the party could be seen.

He also said the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) — a scheme that the PPP often takes credit for launching — was not “anyone’s personal programme but the government’s”.

Earlier on Saturday, PPP leader Saeed Ghani alleged that the PML-N had never won a general election without rigging.

This followed a press briefing by Punjab’s education and sports ministers, where they said that the chief ministers of Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had nothing to show for their performance.

PML-N never won an election without rigging: Ghani

Addressing a press conference in Karachi, Ghani said, “The PPP did not secure power through rigging in any of the elections held till today.

“On the other hand, however many times the PML-N has secured power, it has not been without rigging.”

Ghani, also the Sindh labour minister, made the allegation as he responded to a PML-N member calling on the PPP to not “give lectures on democracy”.

“If you do not want to give the PPP the right to speak on democracy, then will you give it to Gen Musharraf or Gen Zia, or the leaders created by them?” he quipped, referring to the two former military dictators.

The PPP leader said he “did count the 1985 election”, alleging that PML-N supremo and ex-premier Nawaz Sharif “conspired” against ex-prime minister Mohammad Khan Junejo.

He further claimed that his party “became a target of rigging” in the 1988 and 1990 elections, which resulted in the PML-N winning. He went on to allege that the PPP was again “controlled and prevented from forming a government in Punjab” in 1993.

Ghani alleged that the PPP was restricted to “16-17 seats” in the 1997 general elections, when Nawaz’s PML-N again formed the government.

He contended that although the PPP secured power in 2008, the “PML-N was made to win seats, especially in Punjab, through rigging during Musharraf’s tenure”.

Ghani claimed that the PML-N was “made to win” the 2013 elections as well.

“Then the elections in 2024 [took place]. No matter how many times they say, everyone, even children, know that the PML-N was badly defeated in the elections,” he asserted.

The PPP leader alleged that Nawaz, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz “lost their own seats and then blame us”.

Ghani made the remarks after explaining the rationale for his party’s stances on new provinces in Sindh and Punjab, stressing that it was based on the wishes of the people.

He emphasised that the Constitution required any such move to be made through the elected representatives in the provincial assembly concerned.

He noted that the “people of Sindh, its representatives and its assembly say there is no need for further provinces in Sindh”.

On the other hand, Ghani pointed out, the Punjab Assembly and the Senate had passed resolutions over a decade ago calling for two new provinces in Punjab.

“If the people and the elected representatives of Sindh say that there is no need for any new province in Sindh, then no one in Punjab has the right to say whether there should be a new province in Sindh or not,” Ghani asserted.

He went on to stress that the PPP advocated for more provinces in Punjab as the “people of Punjab and their elected representatives” desired that.

The PPP leader emphasised that his party “represented” the citizens of each of the provinces when taking a stance for Sindh and Punjab.

At the outset of his press conference, Ghani also took exception to comments made by “two ministers”, saying it seemed that they “did not know anything about Sindh”.

“They are restricted within a circle called Maryam Nawaz. They only see and say what she tells them, shows them and explains to them,” he said in an apparent reference to the Punjab ministers.

item.description:
The Dhaka South City Corporation’s decision to allocate Tk 50.5 crore for mosquito control is, on paper, a welcome move. That a pre-monsoon survey found Aedes mosquito larval density above the prescribed index in 63 of its 75 wards, with 27 wards identified as high-risk areas, shows that we must take mosquito control seriously.
Indeed, after years of rising dengue cases, public frustration, and repeated failures in vector management, a larger budget signals recognition of the scale of the problem.
However, Dhaka’s residents have seen this pattern before: Money allocated, announcements made, and yet the city remains overwhelmed by mosquitoes.
This is because a bigger budget means nothing if the implementation remains weak.
The core issue has never been the lack of funds but the lack of planning, coordination, and accountability. The city corporations frequently act reactively, not proactively, responding only after dengue cases surge.
With dengue deaths already occurring, this year’s allocation must break that cycle. Dhaka needs a scientifically guided, year‑round mosquito control strategy, not a seasonal scramble.
That means ensuring that every ward has a clear operational plan along with investing in trained personnel, modern equipment, and transparent reporting so residents can see where and how the budget is being used.
Public engagement is equally crucial. Without community participation -- clearing water containers, maintaining rooftops, reporting breeding sites -- even the best efforts from the city corporation will fall short. Yet, community participation only works when the city corporations lead with consistency and credibility.
We appreciate the increased budget, but as a city, we have no room left for symbolic gestures. With dengue now a near‑permanent threat, promises are not enough. We need to see results.

item.title: Moving up the value chain. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Despite Bangladesh's ready-made garment industry's long history of being the backbone of the country's export economy, it is unfortunate that the sector is still viewed primarily as a source of inexpensive clothing rather than a producer of quality, value-added apparel.
Remaining trapped under the "cheap clothes" label has visibly limited export earnings, weakened competitiveness, and left manufacturers vulnerable to relentless price pressure from international buyers.
This is a challenge that demands urgent attention if Bangladesh hopes to secure the industry's long-term future.
Competing solely on low production costs is no longer a sustainable strategy. Rising wages, increasing compliance requirements, and fierce competition from other manufacturing hubs mean Bangladesh must differentiate itself in ways that extend beyond affordability.
The next phase of growth must therefore be driven by quality, innovation, and branding rather than volume alone -- but achieving this transformation will require a coordinated national effort.
Greater investment in product design, research and development, and modern manufacturing technologies can help factories produce higher-value garments. Workforce development is equally essential, with training focused on advanced production techniques, digital manufacturing, and quality assurance.
At the same time, manufacturers should diversify into technical textiles, performance wear, sustainable fashion, and premium apparel -- sectors that command higher prices and are experiencing growing global demand.
We must also start viewing sustainability as a competitive advantage: Bangladesh has already made impressive strides in green garment manufacturing, and this reputation should be leveraged more aggressively in international markets.
Building stronger domestic fashion brands and expanding direct relationships with global retailers can also reduce dependence on contract manufacturing alone.
The garment sector has repeatedly demonstrated its resilience and adaptability. Now, it must prove that it can evolve beyond being the world's low-cost producer.
By embracing innovation, quality, sustainability, and value addition, Bangladesh can redefine its position in the global apparel market and ensure that its most important export industry continues to thrive for decades to come.

item.title: What looks good, and what actually works. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every year, millions of dollars flow through international development channels with the best of intentions, yet remarkably little of it sticks to the soil.
The structural flaw begins long before a shovel hits the dirt. In the traditional aid pipeline, the power dynamic is inherently top-down: An international donor publishes a rigid call for proposals, and local NGOs rush to design programs that fit the grant's specific criteria.
The process is rarely driven by what a community actually needs; instead, it is driven by what the donor is currently willing to fund. And the most reliably funded intervention of all? Training.
Ask any funder how a training program performed, and the response arrives in a familiar, quantifiable shape: The number of participants, the tally of workshop-days delivered, the stack of certificates issued.
These are the clean, unassailable metrics that populate logical frameworks and final reports -- the boxes donors can easily tick to justify renewing a project.
Donor call becomes NGO proposal becomes short workshop becomes trainer leaving with no follow-up, and yet, on paper, the metric is met.
They are also, far too often, an illusion of progress.
The appearance of success
Certain organizations are attempting to upend this model, starting with a fundamental truth: A true permaculture design cannot be handed over in an afternoon. It requires an intimate, localized understanding of a specific plot of land. It requires testing soil and water through a full cycle of seasons, adjusting the strategy when it fails the first time, and ensuring a knowledgeable guide remains present to see those adjustments through.
Making compost and mixing organic fertilizer are the easy parts of sustainable agriculture -- and, crucially, they are the parts that photograph well for a donor's quarterly newsletter. But the actual design process -- the patient, gritty substance of permaculture -- is precisely what gets sacrificed when success is measured in workshop-days rather than seasons.
This pattern is hardly unique to agriculture. It is the same mechanism that produces vocational training programs with high enrollment but near-zero career placement, governance workshops with packed rooms but zero institutional reform, and "capacity building" initiatives that build no real capacity beyond the expiration date of the contract.
Output-based funding structures naturally select for interventions that are visible, short-term, and exportable -- not those that are embedded, patient, and hard to quantify.
Inside the Sundarbans
Few people understand this disconnect better than Rosemary Morrow. She has spent nearly five decades teaching permaculture in the volatile margins where traditional development programs eventually move on -- refugee camps, drought-stricken farms, and war-affected communities across three continents.
For almost a decade, she has partnered with local NGOs to establish permaculture structures in Bangladesh's ecologically fragile Sundarbans region.
Alongside Joyti Halder, a development worker with decades of NGO experience spanning the Rohingya refugee camps and the tea gardens of northern Bangladesh before returning to her home district in the Sundarbans, I visited a number of households in the region that had undergone training.
The pattern was starkly consistent. A facilitator had arrived, taught for a few days, and left. In several cases, the implementing NGO remained active in the area -- staff still visiting, still filing reports -- yet no one had returned to the households themselves to see whether anything had taken root. The training had been officially delivered. It had also, functionally, disappeared.
Halder has seen this pattern play out for decades, and worse. "I have been working in the NGO sector for decades, and it's often devastating. Aid money seems to vanish. There is much corruption in the current system," she says.
She recalls a trainer during permaculture work in the Rohingya camps who was tasked with buying old cement sacks for sack gardens -- a pragmatic way to grow vegetables where no land is available -- and simply pocketed the difference between the real price and what he reported.
"Inflating bills is a common phenomenon in Bangladesh. It's the easiest way to steal money from a donor. Many NGO founders have become quite rich that way."
For Halder, the deeper issue is structural: "It's us on the ground who should develop the necessary programs and budgets and reach out to donors. It doesn't make sense for an international donor to promise a fixed amount -- often in the hundreds of thousands of euros or dollars -- and have local NGOs build their programs and budgets around that number."
What Morrow and Permafund Australia have pushed for instead costs almost nothing. Not a single taka of their funding has gone into traditional infrastructure. There is no dedicated training centre, no rented conference facility, no multi-year consultant contract, no five-star hotel.
Instead, the model relies on training embedded directly within the community, led by people the village already knows and trusts. In several Sundarbans villages, this has meant identifying quiet, self-starting individuals -- some with only a few weeks of prior training, unsupported and unrecognized until now -- and investing in their capacity to lead, rather than importing an outside facilitator on a fixed itinerary.
This is a difficult model for large institutions to fund, for one uncomfortable reason: It offers no clean deliverable. There is no single training event to photograph, no easily tabulated "number of people reached" to present to a board.
What it produces instead is durability -- the one thing every evaluation framework claims to want, but almost never actually measures.
Redefining the results framework
Fixing the broken mechanics of international aid does not require a larger influx of capital. It arguably requires less: Fewer per-diem-heavy facilitator rotations, fewer permanent training compounds, fewer glossy midline reports that serve the bureaucracy rather than the people.
Instead, it requires funders with the institutional courage to back something that looks, in year one, like almost nothing happening at all.
It means quietly providing a resourceful resident of a Sundarbans village with the materials, respect, and recognition to keep doing exactly what they were already doing -- unpaid and unnoticed -- long after the workshop banners have been taken down and packed away.
That is a difficult thing to fit into a modern results framework. It may also be the only thing genuinely worth putting in one.
Julia Wesemann is Director, Growing Together.

item.title: The trillion taka enterprise opportunity we aren’t seizing. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every Bangladeshi family knows this scene: A relative falls ill, and while public hospitals remain the backbone of care for millions, they often operate under intense demand. Private care, meanwhile, is generally faster but financially difficult for ordinary households. In between these two worlds sits a gap that Bangladesh has not yet learned to see as what it is: A market waiting for entrepreneurs, and specifically for women entrepreneurs, to build the businesses that fill it.
Bangladeshi women are already the informal architects of family health. They notice symptoms, care for children and elderly parents, arrange medicines, accompany relatives to clinics, manage food and recovery, and manage household budgets when illness strikes.
What they have not been given is the entrepreneurial infrastructure to turn that expertise into enterprise: The training, capital, platforms, and institutional trust that would let this informal knowledge become paid, scalable, professional work.
That is the opportunity now sitting in front of the country.
The World Health Organization reports that Bangladesh’s Universal Health Coverage service coverage index stands at only 54 out of 100, while 41.7% of the population faced financial hardship from out-of-pocket health expenditure in 2025.
Read as a policy statistic, this is a warning. Read as a founder would read it, it is something else: A large, underserved market with a clear willingness to pay for something better, and no dominant player who has solved it yet.
Bangladesh already has proof that this model works at scale. Brac’s oral rehydration therapy campaign in the 1980s trained female health workers to visit millions of households and teach mothers how to prepare life-saving treatment at home, helping Bangladesh achieve one of the world’s highest oral rehydration therapy (ORT) use rates.
Decades later, Brac’s network of 100,000 trained women community health workers continues to show that women can operate as trusted, effective distribution channels between households and the health system. Strip away the language of development programming, and what you have is a validated go-to-market model: Community-based, women-led, high-trust, low-cost, and provably capable of scaling nationwide. Few ventures anywhere are handed evidence this strong that their model works.
The question is why Bangladesh has treated this as a public health legacy rather than as the foundation of an entire entrepreneurial sector.
The future of care in Bangladesh should not be imagined only through hospitals, doctors, and digital platforms. It should be imagined through the small enterprises women could build around it: Community wellness navigation services, maternal and child health coordination, mental health awareness outreach, eldercare assistance, pharmacy-linked guidance, home-based diagnostics coordination, nutrition counselling, and trusted referral networks.
A woman who already supports families informally during illness could become the founder of a trained wellness-navigation service.
A woman entrepreneur could build and run a home sample-collection or maternal-health coordination business. A young graduate could launch a digital referral start-up connecting women and elderly patients to verified providers. A local women’s group could formalize into a micro-enterprise partnering with clinics and pharmacies on chronic disease adherence.
These are not abstract social-good ideas. They are viable business models with real customers, real willingness to pay, and a genuine societal return.
Why start with women?
This is also where the societal-impact case becomes as strong as the commercial one. Women’s participation in enterprise in Bangladesh remains far below its potential, and women-owned small businesses still represent a limited share of the overall business landscape.
A women-led care economy would not just fill a service gap; it would meaningfully expand the number of women running income-generating enterprises in the country, while simultaneously improving health access, reducing household financial hardship, and strengthening community resilience.
Few sectors offer this kind of double return, where the commercial opportunity and the development outcome point in exactly the same direction.
To be clear, the goal is not to convert women’s unpaid care burden into more unpaid work dressed up as opportunity. That would be exploiting the very problem this piece is describing.
The goal is the opposite: To convert existing, undervalued care knowledge into respected, compensated, trained, and institutionally backed enterprises -- with founders who own equity, set prices, hire staff, and build something that outlives any single funding cycle.
Bangladesh’s digital readiness makes this moment particularly opportune. Mobile connectivity and app-based platforms have already reshaped how people manage money, shopping, transport, and education, creating the infrastructure layer that women-led care ventures could build on directly -- for logistics, payments, scheduling, and referral.
But technology alone will not build trust in something as sensitive as family health. Women-led local networks, with their existing community credibility, are the missing distribution and trust layer that no app can manufacture on its own. This is precisely why a well-designed venture, not a well-designed feature, is what is required.
What Bangladesh needs now is not another pilot project that quietly disappears after a funding cycle. It needs a genuine entrepreneurial ecosystem built around this opportunity.
Let us have universities preparing graduates to create and run ventures at the intersection of care, technology, and enterprise; banks and financial institutions underwriting women-led care businesses as legitimate micro and small enterprises rather than as charity cases; healthcare providers partnering with community-based entrepreneurs instead of assuming all care must originate inside formal facilities; and development partners shifting from grant-funded pilots toward investment-ready, scalable business models.
The ingredients are already in the country: Women with deep, lived care expertise; a proven history of community-based health distribution; rising digital infrastructure; unmet and well-documented demand; and institutions capable of coordinating around a shared opportunity.
What has been missing is the decision to treat this as an entrepreneurial sector worth building, not only a social issue worth managing.
Bangladesh should stop asking how to help women cope with the burden of family care, and start asking how to help women build businesses out of the expertise that burden has already given them.
The country should see them not only as caregivers inside the home, but as founders, operators, and builders of one of the most investable, highest-impact sectors it has yet to formally create.
Dr Nusrat Hafiz is an Assistant Professor and Director of the Women Empowerment Cell at BRAC Business School, BRAC University. Her research focuses on entrepreneurship, women’s empowerment, and societal impact in emerging economy contexts.
